Restriction-RL shows higher verified-proof diversity than standard GRPO.

A report on the Lean arm of my exploration experiments, and research into why this exploration method is so interesting for coding and other applications.

Code · August 2026

Contents

  2. Preliminary evidence

Summary

A theorem can have many correct proofs. A reward signal that recognizes only correctness does not tell a model which of those proofs is worth keeping. Restriction-RL asks whether post-training can preserve a broader repertoire by withholding reinforcement from a dominant, already-verified proof mode.

The preliminary comparison is encouraging: 56.8% more observed tactic signatures during training and 14.0% more on held-out theorems than standard GRPO. The proposed research tests whether this broader distribution improves proof search, transfer, and mathematical discovery. [1]

Evidence status. Figure captions distinguish repository measurements and derived calculations from proposed mechanisms, mathematical illustrations, and evaluation budgets. No new model runs are reported here. The current comparison is single-seed and differs in optimization settings, so it does not yet isolate the effect of blocking alone. [1]

Correctness and strategy diversity require separate evaluation.

Consider the elementary inequality 2ab ≤ a² + b². One route starts with a nonnegative square. Another uses convexity at the midpoint. Both arrive at the same result, but they expose different intermediate ideas. Keeping both can matter when the next problem preserves one route and obstructs the other.

A language model’s proof distribution is more complicated than this illustration. Some differences are substantive; others are only formatting, lemma aliases, or a different arrangement of the same algebra. That distinction is central to the project. We want to study a repertoire of useful methods, not merely produce more strings.

The current intervention begins with a tractable proxy: a deterministic signature of the tactic sequence in a Lean-verified proof. A frozen base-policy archive supplies the dominant mode for eligible training theorems. Training then restarts from the base checkpoint. When that mode is sampled again and verifies, its policy advantage is set to zero. The attempt remains in the sample count, retains its verified-correct status, and contributes to the reported compute cost. [1]

This is an intervention on the learning signal, not a ban on generating a proof. Alternative correct attempts and incorrect attempts keep their upstream treatment. The archive is fixed in the present method; an adaptive archive is a proposal developed below. [1]

Working hypothesisReducing the reinforcement assigned to a dominant verified strategy may preserve learning opportunities for alternatives without introducing a learned novelty reward.

Related work gives this question a useful context. Yue and colleagues find that, in their tested settings, RLVR can improve low-budget success while failing to improve the high-budget coverage available from the base model. Cui and colleagues study entropy collapse during reasoning-model RL. These are motivations to measure distributions carefully, not proofs that RL can never learn a new strategy. [6][7]

A complete, authored Lean example

The mathematical illustration above is not a model sample. Here is a compact Mathlib-style encoding of its square-certificate route. It has not been compiled in this environment; the actual repository excerpts appear in Section 3.

import Mathlib

example (a b : ℝ) : 2 * a * b ≤ a ^ 2 + b ^ 2 := by
  nlinarith [sq_nonneg (a - b)]

The convexity route is a different mathematical argument, not evidence of a second model-discovered strategy. Conversely, replacing this one-line proof with several explicit intermediate algebraic steps need not create a new mathematical strategy.

Observed diversity is higher, but capability expansion remains unproven.

The strongest current finding is recovery of observed proof diversity relative to GRPO. The base policy remains an important reference point.

The training comparison covers 9,655 theorems and 308,960 proposals per condition. At the tactic-signature level, restriction observes 53,825 modes against GRPO’s 34,336. At the exact normalized proof level, the counts are 111,570 and 66,515. Both remain below the base archive’s corresponding coverage. [1]

These training counts aggregate an evolving policy, rather than evaluating one final checkpoint. The held-out analysis is therefore more informative about what the trained policy exposes: 223 registered-validation theorems and 244 miniF2F-test theorems, with 32 fresh proposals per theorem. [1]

The effects differ across metrics and sampling budgets. At one draw, restriction has lower success than standard GRPO on both evaluation sets. At 32 draws, the theorem counts are similar: 273 solved across the combined set under restriction, versus 271 under GRPO. A broader sampled repertoire can coexist with a less concentrated first guess. [1]

The two datasets use different vertical-axis ranges.

Most of the solved set is shared. The small number of discordant outcomes does not establish a reliable improvement in theorem-solving capability; the reported exact paired test gives p = 0.727. Nor does a nonsignificant test prove equivalence. [4]

Restriction exposes more proof modes on largely the same theorems.

The paired view separates correct attempts from distinct successful modes. Restriction has more tactic signatures on 187 held-out theorems and fewer on 66, while its number of correct attempts increases on only 57 and decreases on 149. This is why a single success-rate number cannot characterize the change. [4]

Observed coverage differences increase with the sampling budget.

The accumulation curve above makes the distinction visible at different sampling budgets. Its points are rarefaction estimates: expected observed coverage when subsampling the existing 32 attempts without replacement. The restriction advantage grows with the sampled budget, but the base policy still exposes more tactic signatures at 32. There are no measured curves beyond that point in this presentation. [3]

We can also hold the number of correct draws fixed. Among the common eligible held-out theorems, 16 correct draws expose an estimated 10.27 tactic modes under restriction, 9.14 under GRPO, and 11.33 under the base policy. The comparison suggests a distributional difference beyond simply producing a different number of correct samples. [3]

Coverage gains persist across encodings but do not establish semantic diversity.

The direction survives six frozen representations, from the first tactic head to exact normalized proof text. That is a useful robustness check. It does not turn a syntactic measure into a semantic one: several signatures may encode the same idea, and the same signature may hide different lemma choices or subgoal structures. [3]

Exploratory difficulty strata sharpen the next research question. The largest mean gain in tactic signatures occurs on theorems where the base policy already succeeds 17–31 times out of 32. The immediate opportunity may be to turn alternative methods for relatively familiar problems into resources for harder ones—not to assume that broader sampling already solves the hard problems. [4]

Restriction slows the observed increase in concentration during training.

The opening richness figure shows the gap emerging early across successive training windows. These are equally sized windows with changing theorem populations, not repeated measurements on a fixed evaluation panel. The phase portrait below complements that view by combining two summaries: the dominant mode’s share and the effective number of modes among correct samples. [2]

Both policies become more concentrated. Restriction slows that process in this comparison; it does not abolish it. This is an important distinction when designing a controller that must keep working after the first dominant mode has been suppressed. [2]

What the diversity statistics mean

A mode is counted within a theorem: the same tactic sequence on two different theorems contributes two theorem–mode pairs. For a theorem with N sampled attempts and nₘ occurrences of a correct mode, its probability of appearing in a without-replacement subsample of size k is 1 − C(N − nₘ, k) / C(N, k). Summing over modes and theorems gives the accumulation estimate.

For correct-mode frequencies pₘ within a theorem, the Simpson effective-mode count is 1 / Σₘ pₘ². A value of three means the concentration matches that of three equally frequent modes, not necessarily that exactly three distinct proofs were observed. Conditioning on correct draws and reporting the population eligible for that conditioning are both essential.

Raw counts and endpoint values come from the repository summaries. Ratios and plotted indices are calculated from those values. No synthetic error bands or simulated theorem-level observations are added. [3][2]

Recovered modes include rewriting, arithmetic, and intermediate constructions.

The base archive lets us ask a concrete question: which correct modes appeared before training, disappeared from GRPO’s finite sample, and reappeared under restriction? The recovery analysis applies the same question at several minimum base-frequency thresholds. [2][3]

The repository also records inspectable examples. They include direct rewriting with a trigonometric identity, polynomial normalization followed by nonlinear arithmetic, congruence, positivity, and explicit nonnegativity certificates. The relevant Mathlib tactics are documented independently; their success in a particular excerpt depends on the original goal and hypotheses. [2][17]

These are selected top recovered examples, not a random sample of the corpus. Their occurrence counts describe a tactic mode on one theorem, rather than necessarily the identical full proof string. The source reports them as Lean-correct but does not include each complete theorem statement in this compact artifact. We have not recompiled them here. [2]

Two examples beginning with ring_nf → nlinarith use different hypotheses. Two beginning with simp → ring use different rewrite rules. A transition atlas makes the local repertoire easier to inspect while also showing the limits of tactic heads as a representation. [2]

Recovering a previously suppressed mode does not establish sustained diversity; that mode may subsequently become dominant.

In two of these selected examples, the recovered mode occurs in all 32 restriction samples. That is a particularly useful clue: a fixed blocklist can redirect concentration rather than continuously regulate it. This motivates the first algorithmic direction below, but the examples alone do not prove that the replacement effect is widespread. [2]

The research program must connect diversity to learning and practical utility.

The proposal is to treat the distribution of verified strategies as something we can measure, control, and preserve—not merely as a side effect of maximizing reward.

Three claims should be kept separate. Recovery means previously observed behavior is sampled again. Expansion means a model exposes useful strategies or solved problems beyond a carefully measured baseline. Utility means those strategies improve downstream search, robustness, or learning efficiency. The current results speak most directly to recovery. Claims of expansion and utility require separate evidence.

The most promising sequence is to establish causality and semantic validity, build an adaptive controller, then test whether the resulting repertoire improves search and transfer at matched cost. Curriculum and consolidation are higher-upside extensions once those prerequisites hold.

Research priority 1: Causal identification and measurement

Matched controls must isolate the intervention and validate strategy diversity.

Before optimizing a diversity metric, establish what changes it. The next comparison should hold initialization, reference policy, optimizer settings, proposal budget, and sampling fixed while toggling restriction. A random mask with the same theorem-level masking rate is an important control: deleting learning signal is not the same hypothesis as deleting dominant-mode learning signal.

Hypothesis. Dominance-targeted restriction yields a larger increase in audited strategy diversity than a matched random mask, without exceeding a prespecified cost or success-rate tolerance.

The semantic audit should go beyond tactic heads. Collect normalized dependency sets, intermediate goal states, and proof-tree structure, then have blinded reviewers label a stratified sample of proof pairs. Use harmless renamings and equivalent rewrites to test invariance. A representation should merge cosmetic variants while distinguishing materially different decompositions. There need not be one perfect semantic partition: report agreement across several resolutions and document their failure cases.

Decisive test
A fixed, independently sampled proof bank for matched checkpoints. Compare audited strategy coverage and mode probabilities, with sampling uncertainty separated from training-seed variation.
Failure signal
The gain vanishes under matched optimization, is reproduced by random masking, or disappears when superficial variants are merged.

A small bounded benchmark with known proof families would be particularly valuable. It provides a controlled setting in which missing support and repeated variants can be measured directly before making stronger claims on open-ended mathematics.

Research priority 2: Adaptive concentration control

Adaptive control should respond as new strategies become dominant.

The fixed archive is simple and auditable, but it becomes stale. A more capable loop would periodically estimate which verified strategies dominate, reduce reinforcement on overrepresented strategies, and restore it when dominance recedes. The controller should preserve a usable alternative-correct signal rather than applying restriction indiscriminately.

The repository’s offline cross-fit analysis is a useful starting point. It checks whether the unique top mode agrees across two independent halves of a base sample and then requires enough retained alternative-correct attempts. Between 1,961 and 2,425 training theorems pass the displayed variants of this filter. That is evidence of feasibility for an eligibility rule—not evidence that adaptive training already works. [5]

One proposed soft rule uses the estimated share p̂ₘ of strategy m among correct attempts on a theorem. Above a target share τ, reduce its positive advantage gradually rather than always setting it to zero.

wₘ = clip[(τ / (p̂ₘ + ε))α, wmin, 1]Proposed rule: apply wₘA only to positive advantages of correct attempts. Leave incorrect attempts and nonpositive advantages with their upstream treatment. Here α controls sharpness, ε avoids division by zero, and wmin limits suppression. This deliberately changes the objective; it is not an unbiased estimator of ordinary GRPO.

Independent audit samples should estimate concentration on training theorems; evaluation theorems must remain outside the feedback loop. Update the controller on a slower schedule than the policy. Add hysteresis, cooldowns, a minimum correct-signal floor, and a release rule when alternatives are too uncertain. Log every eligibility and weighting decision so the intervention can be replayed.

Decisive test
Compare fixed blocking, stable cross-fit blocking, and soft adaptive weighting at matched resources. Track replacement dominance, audited mode coverage, pass@k, and the fraction of updates with useful positive signal.
Failure signal
The controller oscillates between modes, reinforces syntax gaming, starves difficult theorems of signal, or buys diversity only through a disproportionate correctness loss.

Token-entropy controls and pass@k-oriented advantage design are important baselines, not straw opponents. Existing work addresses exploration at those levels; the proposed distinction here is to intervene on verified strategy concentration within a problem. [7][8]

Research priority 3: Cost-matched proof search

Alternative strategies must improve proof search under a fixed compute budget.

A larger archive matters only if it helps solve something. The direct experiment is to keep a proof-search algorithm fixed and vary the policy that proposes its steps. Compare standard sampling with selection that avoids repeatedly expanding semantically equivalent candidates. The resource unit must include generated tokens, Lean calls, failed checks, and timeouts—not just successful completions.

Hypothesis. A less concentrated proposal policy improves success per verification budget on problems where multiple decompositions lead to different downstream opportunities.

Subgoal decomposition is a natural interface. DeepSeek-Prover-V2 explicitly uses subgoal-based proof construction; recent work on AI-driven formal proof search also motivates evaluating complete research workflows rather than isolated short completions. Neither establishes the benefit of restriction, but both make this a concrete integration target. [9][10]

Use a two-by-two design: baseline versus restriction-trained policy, crossed with ordinary versus diversity-aware search. This distinguishes gains from the learned distribution from gains due to the search scheduler. Evaluate new theorems, first-proof cost, verification calls per solved theorem, and failed-subgoal revisits. Keep the same search budget and prove that the comparison is not merely using more candidates.

Decisive test
Cost-matched success on held-out theorem families, with separate tests that remove a convenient lemma, restrict an allowed library, or alter the decomposition while preserving the mathematical task’s intent.
Failure signal
Coverage rises but search cost does not fall, harder theorems do not improve, or every additional mode shares the same brittle dependency.

The ambitious outcome is a learned portfolio of routes: a model that can switch from a convenient library theorem to a constructive argument, or from a direct certificate to a reusable subgoal decomposition. That remains a target, not an interpretation already licensed by tactic counts.

Research extension 4: Curriculum and discovery

Curricula should test whether alternative strategies support new theorem families.

Restriction mainly redistributes reinforcement over available successes. To expand the frontier, couple it to a curriculum that supplies informative tasks and intermediate lemmas. A proposer could suggest small theorem variations or useful subgoals; a verifier certifies solutions; a difficulty estimator decides which tasks are challenging but learnable.

Absolute Zero provides a relevant proposer–solver self-play precedent. Separately, Cai and colleagues’ curriculum method uses pass@k estimates to locate a boundary, introduces targeted teacher guidance, then consolidates with RL. The teacher contribution matters: it must not be relabeled as spontaneous invention by pure RL. [11][12]

Hypothesis. Near-frontier curricula and restriction are complementary: the curriculum supplies new intermediate knowledge, while restriction reduces the chance that consolidation compresses it back into one familiar route.

A factorial experiment should vary curriculum and restriction separately. Start with small formal domains where task equivalence and dependency overlap are tractable. Reject duplicates, vacuous statements, and tasks made easy by accidentally exposed solutions. Hold out entire theorem/dependency families before generating the curriculum. Teacher-generated and self-generated tasks need separate accounting.

Decisive test
Newly solved held-out families and verified reuse of newly learned lemmas, compared at matched teacher tokens, proposer work, solver work, and verification cost.
Failure signal
Apparent progress comes from restatements, contaminated dependencies, trivial task generation, or teacher information that the baseline never received.

The longer-term prospect is a library-building loop in which diverse proof attempts reveal reusable intermediate structure. Its success criterion should be downstream reuse and reduced proof cost, not simply the number of accepted lemmas.

Research extension 5: Retention and consolidation

Consolidation must retain alternative strategies after restrictions are removed.

An exploratory policy and a deployable policy need not be trained identically. Separate discovery from consolidation: maintain a verified archive, choose examples to cover strategies rather than mirror their raw frequency, and distill them into a policy whose first-attempt performance remains useful. Then remove the archive from inference and test what survived.

The archive can retain proof context, approved dependencies, cost, and a hierarchy of strategy labels. Compare ordinary frequency-weighted replay with theorem-balanced and strategy-balanced replay at equal training-token budgets. Evaluate retained strategies after subsequent RL, including ones that temporarily cease to be optimal for average reward.

Quality-diversity methods such as MAP-Elites offer an analogy for retaining high-quality solutions across distinct behavior classes. GFlowNets provide a different possible baseline: sample structured objects in proportion to reward instead of concentrating only on the best one. Transferring either idea to proofs requires care about what counts as an object; counting many construction paths to the same proof should not create artificial reward mass. [13][14]

Decisive test
Re-evaluate strategy coverage, pass@1, pass@k, and cost after balanced distillation and again after later RL. Use the same held-out proof bank and a separate transfer set.
Failure signal
Diversity exists only while an external archive supplies answers, disappears during consolidation, or survives only by sacrificing an unacceptable amount of first-attempt reliability.

This track turns a temporary sampling effect into a test of durable learning. A verified archive is useful infrastructure; it is not by itself evidence that the model has internalized a repertoire.

Cross-cutting priority 6: Mechanism and verification

Mechanism and trust audits must distinguish diversity from reliability.

A fixed audit bank can distinguish several mechanisms: probability mass moving toward alternative proofs, a mode becoming too rare to observe, representation changes masquerading as novelty, or improved ability to compose familiar components. Measure checkpoint likelihoods on the same proof bank alongside fresh samples. Token-level entropy and strategy-level concentration should be recorded together, not treated as interchangeable.

A controlled mechanistic extension would hold the theorem prefix and continuation bank fixed, then test whether interventions on candidate internal features selectively change particular proof families. Such experiments need matched checkpoints and counterfactual controls; a visually compelling activation map alone would not establish a “diversity circuit.”

Trust also depends on the evaluation contract. Lean verifies a formal statement in an environment; it does not decide whether that statement was the intended task. Freeze theorem statements and imports, reject sorry and unapproved axiom dependencies, audit accepted proofs with #print axioms, and sandbox compilation and execution. An approved trust policy can include standard axioms; the point is to make the dependency boundary explicit. [15][16]

Anthropic’s reward-seeker work is a reminder that optimizing a reward signal and learning the intended behavior are different questions. A broader proof repertoire is not an alignment guarantee. A meaningful safety-related experiment would test dependency failures or specification loopholes directly, with unchanged acceptance rules—not infer safety from high diversity. [18]

Decisive test
Audit whether apparently independent routes remain valid under controlled dependency restrictions and whether every accepted solution respects the same immutable verification contract.
Failure signal
“Diversity” increases because the accepted statement changes, the trust boundary expands, or many different-looking proofs exploit one common loophole.

Experiments should establish causality before testing broader applications.

The expensive studies should be gated by cheaper, informative ones. First establish a reproducible targeted effect and a defensible representation. Only then expand to deep sampling, search, curriculum, and retention.

Proposed comparisons, the questions they isolate, and required accounting
ComparisonQuestion it isolatesRequired accounting
Matched GRPO vs fixed restrictionDoes blocking itself change the successful distribution?Same initialization, KL, optimizer settings, proposals, and sampling.
Fixed restriction vs matched random maskDoes targeting dominant modes matter?Match theorem-level mask rates; report active updates and discarded signal.
Fixed vs stable vs soft adaptive restrictionDoes a concentration controller prevent replacement dominance?Charge archive refreshes and independent training-theorem audit samples.
Restriction vs entropy / pass@k objectivesIs strategy-aware control useful beyond existing exploration methods?Equal tuning and training resources; keep decoding comparisons separate.
Policy × search schedulerDoes learned diversity help a fixed downstream search budget?Tokens, verifier calls, timeouts, first-proof cost, and solved theorems.
Curriculum × restriction; replay ablationsCan new knowledge be acquired and retained?Teacher/proposer information, replay tokens, contamination, and later forgetting.

For the first stage, propose at least three independent seeds for the matched baseline, fixed restriction, and random-mask control. Use pilot variability to set the size of the confirmatory study rather than assuming three seeds are statistically sufficient. Keep a frozen held-out set and a separate development set for controller tuning.

Prespecify a primary strategy-diversity endpoint and a correctness/cost guardrail. Report theorem-level paired effects, seed-to-seed variation, and confidence intervals that respect those levels of dependence. Thousands of correlated rollouts are not thousands of independent training runs. The current theorem-level significance tests should not be presented as evidence of robustness across seeds.

Larger sampling budgets require complete generation and verification accounting.

A deeper evaluation is a real research investment. At 467 held-out theorems, moving from 32 to 128 proposals requires 59,776 attempts per checkpoint. At 512 it requires 239,104. Those numbers exclude the token lengths and verifier costs of individual attempts; they are not GPU-hour estimates.

Stage the evaluation: start with the existing budget, increase to 128 on a preregistered comparison, then expand only where the accumulation curves and uncertainty justify it. Keep the fresh-sampling protocol fixed. Do not extrapolate finite-sample rarefaction past its observed pool or confuse a smooth fitted curve with newly measured support.

Interpretation criterionIf semantic diversity improves but cost-matched search does not, the result is still informative—but the claim should remain “a broader verified distribution,” not “better reasoning.”

Strategic breadth could improve search, transfer, and subsequent learning.

The near-term opportunity is methodological: measure what reward optimization retains and erases. A model can become more likely to answer correctly while exposing fewer methods. A richer evaluation makes that change visible instead of treating every correct completion as interchangeable.

The medium-term opportunity is computational: use a repertoire of verified strategies to allocate search more intelligently. A model that generates alternatives with different dependencies and decomposition choices could avoid repeating the same dead end. This is worth testing because the benefit can be expressed in concrete units—new solved theorems and verification work saved.

The longer-term opportunity is cumulative: discovery produces an archive, the archive supports consolidation, and the consolidated policy supplies better proposals for the next round. Restriction would then be one component of a system for retaining useful knowledge, rather than a permanent prohibition against yesterday’s best proof.

None of those larger outcomes follows from a 14% increase in tactic signatures. The increase provides a measurable starting point in a domain with auditable correctness, inspectable proof objects, and testable criteria for stronger claims.

The central research objective is to determine whether a broader repertoire of verified strategies increases the range of theorems a model can reliably prove.

Measured results and proposed experiments are distinguished throughout.

Measured
Counts, pass@k values, paired summaries, and proof excerpts from the repository’s committed results. The source results document is dated 31 August 2026.
Calculated here
Relative gains, base-indexed coverage, plotted ratios, and proposed evaluation sample counts derived transparently from source numbers.
Authored illustration
The two mathematical routes to an inequality and the full one-line Lean example. They are explanatory examples, not model outputs or new verification runs.
Proposed
Adaptive weighting, semantic audits, search integration, curriculum, archive-balanced consolidation, and the experiment ladder. These are not reported completed experiments.
Scope and limitations of the present comparison

The model in the repository comparison is DeepSeek-Prover-V1.5-SFT. The standard GRPO condition uses one PPO epoch and KL 0.02; the restriction condition uses two epochs and KL 0.10. This confound is why a matched blocking-disabled control is the first proposed experiment. The displayed comparison uses a single seed. [1]

Training summaries aggregate changing on-policy rollouts; final-checkpoint held-out evaluations are distinct. Six complete training windows are shown, omitting the final partial window. The proof examples are deliberately selected high-recovery cases. A zero count means “unobserved in this finite sample,” not “impossible under this policy.” [2]

The presentation uses a selected, manually transcribed extract of public summaries. It does not include raw cluster rollout logs or checkpoints, and no Lean recompilation or model training was performed to create this page. Numeric source values and presentation code are included in the bundle so these figures can be rebuilt and audited.
